evaluation.positioning_hook: In a collapsing small town, a backwoods hunter and a hard-nosed sheriff uncover a government meat program that turns a free picnic into a flesh-eating outbreak.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has an immediate, sellable engine: a government food giveaway becomes a zombie outbreak in a recognizable American town. The audience is clear and genre-proven, though the political satire and rural specificity narrow it a bit from four-quadrant reach.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early and cleanly: free meat, a suspicious acronym, and a town picnic that becomes a mass infection event. The script keeps the premise legible through repeated public rumors, the F.T.A. trucks, and the eventual reveal.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Tyler Conroy is the strongest character on the page — a wild, self-reliant hunter with a contrarian worldview and survival instincts. The supporting cast is functional and colorful, but most of them are built around one-note social positions rather than durable contradiction.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The meat-distribution premise gives the outbreak a distinct political and economic angle, and the script commits to a bleak, satirical small-town ecosystem. It is still operating inside familiar zombie grammar, but the government-food-scarcity frame gives it a sharper identity than a standard infection story.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script steadily escalates from rumor to investigation to public event to full outbreak, and the town-meeting/picnic sequence gives the back half real propulsion. The middle spends a fair amount of time on setup and social texture, but the eventual collapse is staged with clear momentum.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea of a toxic government meat program weaponizing scarcity is fresh and immediately understandable, especially in the opening breadline imagery and the F.T.A. reveal. The outbreak itself is less surprising than the premise that causes it, but the cause-and-effect chain is memorable.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Madigan Grove feels lived-in: unemployment lines, church politics, school lunch, city hall, the sheriff’s office, and the park all feed the same social pressure cooker. The world is story-generating because every institution is strained by scarcity, even before the outbreak hits.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a clear register: rural, cynical, and darkly comic until it turns feral. The tonal blend of small-town satire, political paranoia, and graphic horror is specific, even if some dialogue leans broad.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are real thematic seeds here — scarcity, class resentment, state power, and moral rot — but the script mostly externalizes them through plot rather than deep character interiority. The conspiracy reveal adds scale, though the emotional afterlife is less developed than the premise.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The town has a usable web of relationships — Conroy/Monroe, Hatter/Granger, Jerry/Michelle, Tom/Debbie — and those pairings generate scene energy. Still, the script is driven more by outbreak mechanics than by a truly elastic ensemble system.

lead_characters.name: Tyler Conroy
lead_characters.hook: A wild, self-sufficient hunter who treats the collapse of civilization like vindication. Tyler is the town’s most instinctive survivor and its least socially compliant citizen, a man who trusts meat, rifles, and his own judgment more than institutions; he starts as a local oddball and ends as the only person built for the apocalypse.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Viggo Mortensen in A History of Violence or Josh Brolin in No Country for Old Men — a physically grounded, morally opaque man whose stillness and menace do the work. It gives an actor the chance to play frontier competence, dry humor, and eventual end-of-world fatalism in one role.

lead_characters.name: Clem Monroe
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s-40s, working-class, unemployed auto worker, family man.
lead_characters.hook: Clem is the town’s optimistic everyman, trying to keep dignity intact while unemployment, hunger, and rumor erode the floor beneath him. He’s practical, decent, and easily swayed by hope, which makes him both relatable and tragically vulnerable when the meat finally arrives.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded, humane role that gave Brian Tyree Henry in Causeway or Ben Mendelsohn in Animal Kingdom their emotional authority — a man whose decency makes the collapse hurt more. It offers an actor a chance to play warmth, frustration, and panic without ever becoming the loudest person in the room.

lead_characters.name: Sheriff Hatter
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s-50s, law enforcement, rural small-town authority figure.
lead_characters.hook: A weary sheriff trying to keep order in a town that has already started to fray. Hatter is practical, skeptical, and increasingly outmatched, which gives him a nice arc from local cop to overwhelmed crisis manager as the town’s rules stop meaning anything.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Michael Shannon in Take Shelter or Kyle Chandler in Friday Night Lights their authority — a man trying to project control while the world slips past him. It gives an actor a steady escalation from dry procedural authority into helpless survival.

lead_characters.name: Tom Haster
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s-40s, working-class, gun-obsessed, politically agitated father.
lead_characters.hook: Tom is a combustible believer, equal parts patriot, rumor-monger, and hungry family man. He’s funny until he isn’t, and the script uses him as a pressure valve for the town’s paranoia, then as a tragic victim of the very hope he helps spread.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of volatile supporting turn that gave Walton Goggins in Justified or Shea Whigham in Boardwalk Empire so much juice — a man who can pivot from comic agitation to genuine threat. It offers a strong character actor a chance to make every scene feel one bad decision away from disaster.

lead_characters.name: Debbie Haster
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 30s-40s, working-class mother, alcoholic, small-town wife.
lead_characters.hook: Debbie is the exhausted center of a household that is already cracking before the outbreak arrives. She masks fear with humor and liquor, and the script gives her enough domestic detail to feel like a real woman trapped inside a collapsing family system.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of bruised domestic role that gave Frances McDormand in Fargo or Patricia Clarkson in Pieces of April their texture — a woman whose survival is emotional before it becomes physical. It gives an actor a chance to play resignation, wit, and maternal terror in the same breath.

lead_characters.name: Jerry Nash
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late teens, high-school athlete, working-class youth.
lead_characters.hook: Jerry is the town’s restless adolescent energy, all impulse, hormones, and half-formed morality. He’s not built for the world he’s inheriting, which makes his romance with Michelle and his confrontation with her father feel like a doomed coming-of-age thread inside the larger catastrophe.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of volatile young role that gave Timothée Chalamet in Beautiful Boy or Lucas Hedges in Manchester by the Sea a chance to show rawness under pressure. It offers a young actor a bruised, emotional arc that starts as teen rebellion and ends in survival horror.

lead_characters.name: Michelle Reed
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late teens, high-school student, abuse survivor.
lead_characters.hook: Michelle is the script’s most tragic civilian: pregnant, trapped, and already carrying the damage of her father’s abuse before the outbreak gives her a monstrous second life. She begins as a victim of the town’s private violence and becomes one of its most disturbing public symptoms.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of devastating role that gave Jodie Comer in The Last Duel or Kaitlyn Dever in Short Term 12 their emotional and physical range — a young woman forced to carry trauma, shame, and rage at once. It gives an actor a transformation role with real horror-movie payoff.

lead_characters.name: Pastor Fussel
lead_characters.hook: Pastor Fussel is the town’s moral interpreter, but he’s too soft, too eager, and too easily compromised to hold the line when the crisis turns personal. He wants to be a shepherd, yet he keeps making choices that deepen the damage around Michelle and Jerry.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of conflicted authority role that gave Paul Dano in There Will Be Blood or Michael Stuhlbarg in Boardwalk Empire room to play conscience under pressure. It offers an actor a chance to make piety, guilt, and helplessness all legible in the same performance.

lead_characters.name: Mayor Granger
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 50s-60s, local politician, self-important civic figure.
lead_characters.hook: Granger is a vanity-driven small-town politician who mistakes visibility for leadership. He wants the cameras, the credit, and the optics of generosity, which makes him exactly the wrong man to have near a covert government operation.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of opportunistic civic role that gave Bryan Cranston in Trumbo or Bob Balaban in Gosford Park their comic-authority edge — a man who thinks he’s steering history while history uses him. It gives an actor a chance to play vanity, panic, and bureaucratic self-preservation.

lead_characters.name: Deputy White
lead_characters.hook: White is the junior lawman who starts as support and ends up as the town’s last thin line of resistance. He’s eager, decent, and increasingly out of his depth, which makes his survival thread useful as a witness to the collapse.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of escalation role that gave Jesse Plemons in Friday Night Lights or John Boyega in Attack the Block their early-career lift — a younger man learning competence under fire. It gives an actor a clean arc from sidekick to reluctant survivor.

lead_characters.name: Arlo Hawk
lead_characters.hook: Hawk is the polished face of the operation, calm enough to sell relief while hiding a mass-casualty program underneath it. He’s the script’s most overt institutional villain, a man who can speak in civic language while executing a population-control plan.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of controlled antagonist role that gave Michael Shannon in Boardwalk Empire or Giancarlo Esposito in Breaking Bad their menace — a man whose calm is more frightening than shouting. It gives an actor a chance to play bureaucratic evil with military precision.

casting_characteristics: one child actor with a major transformation sequence

notable_requirements: small-town park with large crowd capacity
residential homes with practical yard space

technical.vfx_details: Primarily practical gore and crowd transformation effects; no major digital environments or creature work indicated.
technical.sfx_needs: Blood effects, bite makeup, prosthetic wounds, vehicle impacts, gunfire, and practical outbreak makeup on multiple performers.

rights_flags.detail: President Moore is a fictional president, but the script references Soviet Chancellor Brakvitch and the U.S. Department of Agriculture as institutions rather than specific living people.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Standalone feature with a commercial horror release model; best suited to theatrical genre distribution or streaming genre acquisition.

budget.note: The town-wide outbreak, crowd scenes at the park, multiple gore beats, vehicle work, and practical transformation effects keep this above a simple contained indie, but it remains scopeable without heavy VFX.

casting.note: Tyler Conroy needs a very specific blend of frontier charisma, menace, and deadpan humor, while Michelle requires a young actor who can carry abuse, pregnancy, and a horror transformation. Those are strong roles, but they narrow the pool.

development.note: The premise is clear, but the script leans on a large ensemble of town types and a late conspiracy reveal, so the buying conversation will center on whether the satire, horror, and political angle are all landing at feature scale.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adult horror audiences who like outbreak movies with a political edge and a rural Americana setting.
audience_target.demographics: 18-44 skew, male-leaning but accessible to genre couples and horror fans who respond to social satire.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary small-town locations, practical gore, crowd scenes, and vehicle work push it above micro, but the lack of heavy VFX or period build keeps it in indie feature territory.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the elevated-genre lane: a contained but socially legible horror premise with a clear hook, practical effects, and a strong small-town identity. The political-satire layer gives it a little more buyer conversation than a standard infection movie without pushing it out of the genre lane.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature. The world is usable, but there is no clear sequel or spinoff vector beyond a generic continuation of the outbreak.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The meat giveaway is a killer hook.
strengths.what_it_means: This gives the project a one-sentence commercial identity that is easy to pitch, easy to market, and easy to remember. Buyers looking for a genre title with a clean premise can understand the engine immediately.
strengths.evidence: The repeated rumor of free meat, the F.T.A. trucks, and the town meeting all build toward the picnic reveal.

strengths.what_it_means: The unemployment lines, food distribution, church chatter, and civic desperation create a world that feels economically specific rather than generic apocalypse wallpaper. That texture helps the movie feel timely and gives the horror a social bite.
strengths.evidence: The opening breadline imagery, the unemployment office, and the repeated talk of hunger and sacrifice.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Tyler Conroy is a strong genre lead.
strengths.what_it_means: He gives the movie a face and a point of view that can carry posters, trailers, and audience memory. A buyer can package around a rugged, iconoclastic survivor who feels distinct from standard cop-or-soldier protagonists.
strengths.evidence: His deer hunt, his contempt for processed food, and his calm competence once the outbreak starts.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The outbreak set-piece is big and readable.
strengths.what_it_means: The picnic sequence gives the film a clear midpoint-to-third-act engine that can deliver the kind of crowd chaos genre buyers want. It also offers practical production value without requiring expensive VFX-heavy spectacle.
strengths.evidence: The park barbecue, the first sickness wave, and the rapid spread of ghouls through the crowd.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The conspiracy reveal adds a second layer.
strengths.what_it_means: The F.T.A. / foreign toxic agent twist turns the movie from simple infection horror into a government-sabotage thriller, widening the appeal to audiences who like paranoia and institutional betrayal. That gives the ending a sharper aftertaste than a purely accidental outbreak.
strengths.evidence: The sentry’s explanation in the forest and the revelation that the meat was the delivery system.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, marketable outbreak movie with a memorable hook, a strong rural identity, and a contained production footprint that fits the elevated indie horror lane. The premise is commercial on its face, but the small-town scarcity texture and government-conspiracy turn give it enough specificity to stand out in a crowded genre field.

items.area: The ensemble is broader than the engine needs.
items.detail: The script spends a lot of time on town types — the pastor, the mayor, the sheriff, the teens, the families — before the outbreak fully pays off. That gives the world texture, but it also means the buying conversation will center on whether the movie is truly Tyler’s story or a wider social mosaic.

The F.T.A. meaning and the military explanation land deep into the back half, after the audience has already been asked to invest in rumor and civic panic. That delay is not fatal, but it does mean the script relies on patience before the central mechanism fully clicks into place.

items.area: Several supporting roles read as types.
items.detail: Tom, Debbie, Jerry, Michelle, Granger, and Fussel all have clear functions, but many are built around a single social note or dramatic function rather than a layered contradiction. That keeps the script moving, but it limits the long-tail appeal of the ensemble in packaging conversations.

items.area: The gore and crowd work are tier-sensitive.
items.detail: The picnic outbreak, mass infection, and multiple transformation beats will require disciplined practical effects, stunt coordination, and crowd management. It is still an indie feature, but the production will need to protect scope carefully to avoid drifting upward in cost.

issues.headline: The main friction is not concept — it’s balance: the script has enough town texture to feel alive, but that same sprawl makes the lead focus and the conspiracy mechanics feel slightly delayed. On the production side, the park outbreak and crowd contagion are the moments that will need the most discipline to keep the movie inside its lane.
